why: Taste rule 'name the actor': A's concrete subject 'The LLM knows the design of famous sites by name' beats B's passive inversion, which is also wordier and awkward.
Shorter, and A's 'scan your calendar for the next two weeks' is the plainer phrasing; B adds 'If you are stuck' and 'biggest' with no gain (fewer words read faster).
'Ask it for a plan' is plainer than 'Request a plan from it'; the difference is small and mostly familiarity, but A is the shorter, more natural phrasing.
'If a line is empty' vs 'When a line is blank' and 'fill it with' vs 'fill it in with' are interchangeable wording; no taste rule favours either.
'If unsure, check before you upload' is shorter and a plain imperative; 'When in doubt, check before uploading it' adds words (shorter wins, tn-read-the-shapes).
'combine clues stored apart' is more precise and shorter than 'join clues that sit in different places' (fewer words read faster).
Reordering only; no rule or past call separates them, word count is equal.
Shorter by one word, 'without any files' vs 'that has no files'; fewer words read faster.
Divide/run in parallel/bring back vs split/side by side/return: plain-word swaps, no rule clearly followed or broken.
Separate vs Divide an agent handling two jobs: neither follows a named rule; A is shorter by a word but not a removed clause.
'One test that passes' vs 'A single passing test' is a near-equivalent rewording with the same length; no taste rule favors either.

'Mitigations for agents come on top of normal company controls, not instead of them' names the actor plainly and reads clearer than the abstract 'Agent mitigations are added to... not used in place of' (concrete subject, plain words).
Names the concrete actor and says what the report contains; A's 'is found in the report' is passive and vaguer.
'Scope it down' vs 'Narrow it' with 'ends up safe' vs 'is both safe' are wording preferences; no rule or past call separates them.
Only 'support all that the claim says' vs 'back everything the claim states' differs; no rule or past call separates them.

'Compare it with my work contract' is the literal act, whereas 'verify it against my employment contract' implies full verification; this follows the verb-precision rule and the author's preference for plain words.
B's 'They learn from confident, specific, fluent text' is plainer and shorter, and it names the actor; A's 'Their training text is confident…' is more abstract and wordy.

B uses the plain 'Asking the agent... produces' construction with fewer words and a concrete action; A's 'When you ask… it gives' adds clause overhead, so shorter wins (tn-read-the-shapes: fewer words read faster).
Difference is 'Any later run, on any topic, begins from' vs 'The following run, whatever the topic, starts with'; both equal length and register, no rule or past call separates them.
'let you press send' is plainer than 'permit the agent to hit send'; 'permit' is formal and adds a duty/permission-granting tone, and the author prefers plain everyday words and fewer words.
Differences are wording-level (grounded claim can still be vague vs. even a grounded claim can be vague, passes vs. lets pass); same length and meaning, no rule or past call separates them.
'This does not work for a system' vs 'That will not work for a system' is a near-equivalent phrasing swap; no taste rule or past call favours either.
Only difference is 'does not compete with nothing' vs 'is not up against nothing'; no taste rule or past call separates them.
B is shorter and has a concrete subject ('Each picked candidate should state'). A's 'Every candidate you pick should name' is wordier and reads more like duty framing.
Only 'must keep it running... when it is wrong' vs 'someone has to... when it goes wrong'; no taste rule or past call separates them.

'a name does not move inside a folder' is the plainer literal act; B's 'travel' is a slightly more figurative verb and 'has a name on it' adds nothing, so A has fewer words and a tighter metaphor (metaphor-must-fit-its-noun).
Only a clause reorder ('The SHA check from Module 6 was that rule' vs 'In Module 6, the SHA check was that rule'); neither follows or breaks a rule or past call.
'Disagrees; redrafts' keeps plain concrete verbs with no loaded or abstract change. 'Objects/revises' is a near-synonym swap, so this is a weak call between the two.
Only 'Lacking the sponsor... marks' vs 'With no sponsor present... labels'; no taste rule clearly favors either.
Shorter, and 'because' ties the local files to the forum's separate folder; B's wording is smoother but not clearly better.
